title: Token budget & routing intake - Nimbus Payments
summary: Initial discovery focused on per-token unit economics, how batching and KV-caching could fit into Nimbus' payments fraud detection pipelines, and tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private (VPC/on-prem). Customer wants a cost model and a short benchmark on their 1k reqs/min workload. They raised compliance (SOC2, KMS) and data residency concerns; AE to send pricing worksheet and security pack, SE to propose benchmark plan.
action_items: Ayesha Patel: Send hosted vs dedicated cost worksheet and example invoices (due 2026-05-18)
Marco Ruiz: Draft benchmark plan for 1k reqs/min, include KV cache and batching tests (due 2026-05-19)
Priya Desai / Nimbus: Share sample prompt templates and request size distribution (due 2026-05-17)
next_steps: Schedule 1-hour benchmark kickoff (AE + SE + Nimbus infra) week of 2026-05-25
Provide security pack (SOC2 report, SSO/SAML docs, KMS integration notes)
Agree on success criteria for pilot: < $0.002/token effective cost under 200ms p95 for common routes (tentative)
Optional: NDA/POC agreement via CRM link provided by AE
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Ayesha Patel (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Jonah Kim (Nimbus Head of Platform), Priya Desai (Nimbus ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (CTO)

[00:00] Ayesha: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call — hi Jonah, Priya, Liam, and Marco from my side. We wanted to understand your token budget and how you think about routing across hosted/dedicated/private. Is that still right?

[00:12] Jonah: Yeah that's right. We are looking at productionizing an LLM-based fraud signal enrichment. It's not full chat, more like short prompts to augment transaction metadata. So per-request tokens are smaller, maybe 120 to 450 tokens depending on the enrichment. The budget side is big for us— we have tight margins.

[00:35] Marco: Got it. That token distribution is helpful. When you say budget, is that a hard spend cap monthly or more a target per-transaction cost you need to hit?

[00:45] Jonah: It's both. We have a quarterly budget bucket for infra spend—roughly $50k/month for all inference and embeddings. Also product needs per-transaction economics < $0.0015 effective cost ideally. That's kind of the north star.

[01:02] Priya: And there are real-time latency constraints. Fraud enrichment needs to return within 250ms p95 for the fast path, otherwise we degrade to a cached rule. So batching helps cost but can't blow past latency SLO.

[01:20] Ayesha: Good, that's the tradeoff we expect. Quick high-level: Redwood Hosted gives fastest onboarding and simple per-token billing. Dedicated gives reserved GPUs with predictable throughput and lower unit cost at scale, and Private (VPC/on-prem) is for isolated networks and stricter compliance. We'll talk about specific numbers after we see your request mix.

[01:45] Liam: On compliance, we need SOC2, SSO via SAML, KMS integration for keys, and data residency in EU for a subset. We may tilt Private for the EU region if latency demands are strict.

[02:05] Marco: Notes on compliance: hosted customers can get SOC2 and bring-your-own-key via KMS integrations in some configs, but true network isolation (no egress) is Dedicated/Private. We can share the security pack after the call.

[02:20] Jonah: Great. On the economics front, we're curious about effective cost-per-token after applying batching, prefix/KV cache for repeated context, and quantization. How much can Redwood reduce the raw per-token price with those levers?

[02:38] Marco: Short answer: it depends on your hit rate for cache and the batching window. For short prompts like yours, KV cache helps if many requests share prefix or repeated user history; batching helps when you can tolerate small added latency — we have continuous batching that can cut per-token GPU time significantly. Typical multipliers we see: 1.2x-3x effective reduction depending on workload patterns.

[03:00] Priya: Do you have a worked example? Say 1k reqs/min, average 250 tokens, 80% cache hit, and 50ms added latency budget for batching—what does that look like?

[03:15] Marco: We can run numbers. Off the cuff: with high cache hit and small batching windows, you could move from, say, $0.0008/token hosted nominal to an effective $0.00035–0.0005/token. But you need to validate with your exact prompts and sequence lengths. We'll include a spreadsheet with model+batching scenarios.

[03:43] Liam: That delta would be huge. Our CFO will ask for concrete invoice analogs.

[03:50] Ayesha: We'll attach example billing for a few customers with similar profiles (anonymized). Also we'll propose a dedicated baseline if you expect sustained throughput — often dedicated reduces per-token CPU/GPU time because of model residency and fewer multi-tenant overheads.

[04:05] Jonah: Curious about the routing policy. If you have hosted and dedicated, can requests be routed dynamically by latency or cost? For example, small critical requests go to dedicated, bulk async enrichment go to hosted or a lower-cost quantized variant?

[04:20] Marco: Yes, you can implement smart routing rules. Redwood supports policy-based routing — route by latency target, model family, or cost tier. Fallbacks exist if Dedicated capacity is saturated (auto-failover to hosted) but you can set hard caps.

[04:35] Priya: Ok, question on quantization: we run some models with INT8 variants internally. How does Redwood support quantized models and what's the unit cost delta?

[04:45] Marco: We support quantized model variants; they lower memory pressure and per-token compute. Effective cost depends on hardware and model. On some GPUs, INT8/4 quantized variants reduce cost 20–40% versus float16 runs. We'll recommend specific quant profiles in Optimize after seeing model and prompt lengths.

[05:05] Jonah: Sounds good. Another operational question: can we enforce per-route quotas and predictable burst? Our pipeline has spiky periods at end of day settlement windows.

[05:18] Ayesha: Yes — Dedicated lets you configure reserved throughput plus burst capacity. Hosted has rate limits and quotas per account, but with enterprise plans we can configure higher limits and alerts.

[05:30] Liam: For the benchmarking pilot, we want to see p95 latency, tokens/sec, and effective cost. We also want a breakdown: model inference time, queueing/batching overhead, and network egress. Can you produce that?

[05:45] Marco: Absolutely. Our benchmarking template measures token-level latency, batching efficiency, and KV cache hit ratios. We'll instrument and share chronologically: raw model compute, batching window, pre/post processing.

[06:00] Priya: We'll share sample prompts and a synthetic traffic pattern that approximates our peaks. Most requests are stateless but 25% have a short user history attached (so cacheable).

[06:10] Jonah: One more thing on the security piece. For EU-resident data which we want kept in the EU region, what capability is there to force region-specific serving?

[06:22] Marco: You can pin model routes to regions. Hosted supports region selection for endpoints; Dedicated/Private gives you more control and full isolation in-region. If you require customer-managed VPC or an on-prem option for EU-only data, Private is the recommended path.

[06:40] Liam: Who typically owns the VPC setup on Private? Do you assist or is it customer-run?

[06:46] Ayesha: We have an Ops onboarding runbook. For Private VPC we collaborate — customers manage their VPC but Redwood provides a control-plane connector and runbook, plus an initial onboarding window with solution engineers.

[06:58] Jonah: Great. Let's talk numbers more concretely. We're planning a 2-week pilot: 1) functional validation, 2) benchmark for 1k req/min peaks, 3) cost report. What's the minimal Redwood commitment to run that?

[07:12] Marco: For a pilot we often use Hosted to move fast. We can run a scoped dedicated pilot if you want more accurate dedicated numbers; typically a small Dedicated pool for 2 weeks has a minimum but we can sometimes do credits instead. We'll explain the tradeoffs in the worksheet.

[07:30] Priya: If we use Hosted for pilot, will the results extrapolate to Dedicated? We want to avoid surprises when we switch.

[07:38] Marco: They should extrapolate if we account for model residency and different schedulers. We'll include a translation factor in the spreadsheet so you can see estimated dedicated unit cost from hosted pilot metrics. It's not perfect but it's a reasonable projection.

[07:55] Jonah: Ok. On integration: we prefer a single HTTP API, ideally SDK in Go and Python. Any gotchas?

[08:04] Ayesha: We have SDKs in Python, Go, TypeScript and REST. Streaming is supported. We'll link repos and quickstarts.

[08:12] Liam: Regarding observability, can we get token-level cost breakdowns per route and tracing hooks?

[08:20] Marco: Yes, Console offers per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost estimates, tracing, and error logs. For enterprise customers we can give longer retention and integration with S3/Datadog.

[08:35] Priya: A practical nit: how do you compute effective tokens for embeddings vs generation? We use embeddings for similarity lookup and also a small generate step — want to ensure billing matches.

[08:46] Marco: Embeddings are billed per embedding unit (vector creation), generation per token. We'll clarify units in the worksheet and show conversion examples so you can map to your flow.

[09:00] Ayesha: Quick checkpoint — sounds like the pilot scope is clear: 2-week hosted pilot with benchmark traffic, include KV cache and batching variations, deliver p95 latency and cost per token numbers, then extrapolate to dedicated. Any objections?

[09:12] Jonah: No objections. We want to involve finance on the cost extrapolation though. I'll cc our finance lead on the next email.

[09:20] Liam: Also please include notes on SLA and support options if we push to Dedicated later.

[09:26] Ayesha: Will do. Marco, anything else on the technical side?

[09:30] Marco: One thing to flag — if you have a lot of short-lived contexts we might see less caching benefit; but we can often precompute embeddings for common prefixes and reduce calls. Also consider hybrid routing: a smaller model for quick yes/no enrichment and a larger model for deeper enrichments. That reduces average token consumption.

[09:55] Priya: That's interesting — hybrid models could shave a lot. We'll try to classify requests and share the distribution.

[10:02] Jonah: Timebox — we need the security pack and cost worksheet. Can we get those by Monday?

[10:08] Ayesha: Yes — security pack and example invoices by Monday (2026-05-18). Benchmark plan by Tuesday (2026-05-19).

[10:15] Liam: Thanks. Any last questions?

[10:18] Priya: Do you have any customers in payments we can reference?

[10:22] Ayesha: We can share anonymized examples; won't name names on a public copy but we'll include patterns in the worksheet.

[10:28] Jonah: Perfect. Recap then?

[10:30] Ayesha: Recap — Redwood to send: 1) security pack (SOC2, SSO, KMS notes), 2) hosted vs dedicated costing worksheet and sample invoices, 3) benchmark plan. Nimbus to send: sample prompts, request distribution, and finance contact. Schedule benchmark kickoff week of 2026-05-25.

[10:52] Jonah: Sounds good, thanks everyone.

[10:56] Liam: Thanks, bye.

[10:58] (call ends)

Notes on transcript fidelity: automatic captions occasionally mis-labeled acronyms (e.g., 'KV cache' transcribed as 'K V cash' in spots) and timestamps are approximate. There was minor crosstalk when clarifying caching assumptions which the auto-transcript merged.
